sentences.text: Segisaurus was a small, primitive bipedal theropod roughly the size of a goose, measuring approximately 1 meter (3.3 feet) in length.
This dinosaur possessed a bird-like structure with a flexible, elongated neck and a stout body, yet no cranial material was recovered from the specimen.
Charles Lewis Camp likened the posture of the discovered Segisaurus specimen to that of a sitting hen.
Strikingly, a clavicle was found in the Segisaurus specimen, which is unknown in other dinosaurs of that era.
Segisaurus is known only from the holotype UCMP 32101, which was a sub-adult specimen.
The holotype was discovered in 1933 by Max Littlesalt, a Navajo native living in Cañon Tsegi.
Max Littlesalt pointed out the fossils to archaeologists on an expedition after discovering them while keeping livestock in the canyon.
Segisaurus was nimble and insectivorous, though it may have also scavenged meat.
A 2005 re-examination revealed that Segisaurus had hollow bones and that previously identified clavicles were actually fragmented furculae.
Segisaurus possessed three claws and powerful legs that were very long compared to its body, featuring a humeral shaft with stronger torsion and a rectangular humeral deltopectoral crest.
Current reports state that Segisaurus is vital for understanding the evolution of early theropods.
Segisaurus was formally described in 1936 by the paleontologist Charles Lewis Camp based on a fragmentary skeleton consisting of limbs, pelvis, and vertebrae.
Segisaurus belongs to the parent group Coelophysinae and is classified within the family Coelophysidae.
Charles Lewis Camp initially speculated that the neck ribs supported a Draco-like patagium to improve movement, based on the initial misidentification of furculae as clavicles.
Some scientists questioned whether Segisaurus was a theropod because it appeared to have solid bones unlike the hollow bones of Coelophysis, though later studies confirmed it was a coelophysoid.
